content: 1. During the dismantling and transport of installations, hoses should be emptied, preferably dried, and stored in a manner that prevents contamination. 2. All materials used in contact with potable water must be approved for such use. 3. Wastewater management and disposal facilities should be carefully planned and designed to ensure that lavatories and disposal areas are located in a way that avoids any risk of contaminating source water or stored water. 4. Runoff from areas such as livestock pens must be prevented from entering the water source. 5. Covers or roofs should be used to protect water sources from contamination by bird droppings or human activity. 6. Temporary water systems are more vulnerable to accidental or deliberate contamination than permanent systems, necessitating heightened security measures. 7. Water treatment facilities should undergo thorough daily inspections. 8. Operational management documents, which are central to the Water Safety Plan (WSP), should include all procedures and requirements. 9. Signs play a critical role in ensuring proper use of tap water and protecting water sources and drinking-water infrastructure. These signs should be clear, easily understood, and used alongside other barriers, such as fences. 10. Water quality and appearance should be routinely monitored at service taps in temporary water supply systems. 11. At a minimum, daily monitoring of water temperature and disinfectant residuals should be conducted as rapid tests to identify potential issues. 12. Additional parameters, such as pH, conductivity, turbidity, color, and Escherichia coli (or thermotolerant coliforms), should be regularly monitored if possible. 13. Routine sanitary inspections of temporary water supplies by the appropriate health authority are essential. 14. If water quality issues arise, remedial actions outlined in the WSP management documents should be promptly implemented. 15. For temporary water systems used for more than a few weeks, regular surveillance by the health authority should be established. 16. Drinking-water systems in buildings can be significant sources of contamination, and poor management has been linked to disease outbreaks. 17. Ensuring water safety in buildings is challenging because many actions essential to controlling drinking-water quality fall outside the mandate of the water supplier. 18. Roles and responsibilities for managing drinking-water systems in buildings are influenced by factors such as asset ownership and access rights. 19. WSPs for public water supplies typically do not extend to buildings, though they may include initiatives like backflow prevention or consumer education on water quality protection. 20. Building owners, managers, or maintenance personnel are often responsible for managing water supplies, but awareness and application of drinking-water guidelines are frequently limited, necessitating educational support programs. 21. High-risk environments, such as schools, hotels, and large buildings, require heightened vigilance in operational monitoring, validation of control measures, and verification due to the complexity of their water systems and the vulnerability of some users. 22. Maintenance and monitoring programs should be implemented through building-specific WSPs, and compliance may require independent verification and certification by an auditor. 23. The primary hazard to building water systems is contamination from external water supplies or faults in the distribution system, including storage tanks. 24. Unapproved or inappropriate materials can release chemicals into water, with the release varying based on material age and contact duration (e.g., higher lead or copper concentrations in first-draw water). 25. Cross-connections with chemical storage containers, backflow from point-of-use equipment, and connections with non-potable supplies can introduce contaminants into drinking water. 26. Backflow into mains water can occur due to high pressures in connected equipment or low pressures in the mains but can be prevented with appropriate backflow prevention devices. 27. Poor temperature control in water systems can promote the growth of Legionella, which poses an inhalation hazard from spray droplets. 28. In large buildings, long water distribution systems increase the risk of Legionella growth, requiring meticulous maintenance. 29. Effective assessment of health hazards in building water systems requires documentation of the physical structure and system design. 30. Drinking-water systems in healthcare facilities must meet specific quality and treatment requirements, particularly for immunosuppressed patients or specialized uses like dialysis. 31. Microorganisms such as Pseudomonas aeruginosa and mycobacteria, while not typically a concern for the general population, may pose risks to severely immunosuppressed individuals. 32. Water used for medical purposes, such as washing burns or medical devices, may require additional processing like microfiltration or sterilization. 33. Renal dialysis requires water of higher quality than standard drinking water, with special processing to minimize microorganisms, endotoxins, and chemical contaminants. 34. Healthcare facilities should have specific WSPs as part of their infection control programs, addressing water quality, treatment, and microbial growth control. 35. Travelers are at risk of waterborne infections, with diarrhea being the most common symptom, affecting 20–50% of travelers annually. 36. Preventive measures for travelers include drinking only bottled or sealed beverages, avoiding uncooked foods washed with unsafe water, and treating water through boiling, filtration, or chemical disinfection. 37. Boiling water is the simplest and most effective method to kill pathogens, even in turbid water or at high altitudes. 38. If boiling is not possible, chemical disinfection can be effective for clear water, though it may not eliminate all pathogens (e.g., Cryptosporidium oocysts). 39. Chlorineor iodine-based compounds are widely used for water disinfection by travelers, and activated carbon filters can remove excess taste and odor.
